tip: bulamadım = bul (find) + ama (cannot) + dım (I did): I couldn't find. The -ama- slot marks inability, separate from plain negation.
geçen means the one that passed, so geçen ay is last month and geçen hafta is last week. It sits before the time word.
hazırlanmak (to prepare) attaches what you prepare for with dative -a, so you get ready Sınava, for the exam, not sınavı.
yapmayı is yap (do) + ma (the act of) + yı (object mark): the cooking becomes the thing learned. Verbs turn into objects this way.
almadan = al (take) + madan: without taking. Add -madan to a verb stem to say without doing that action.
Gürültüden uses ablative -den to give the cause: because of the noise. The -den ending can mean from or, as here, due to.
öğrenci is öğren (learn) + ci: one who does it, a learner. The -ci ending names the person tied to the action or thing.
Ramazan'da takes an apostrophe before the suffix because Ramazan is a proper name: Ramazan + da becomes Ramazan'da.
Clock times take locative -de for at: yedide means at seven. So saat yedide is at seven o'clock.
şehir drops its second vowel when a suffix follows, so şehir + imiz + de becomes Şehrimizde, in our city, not şehirimizde.
çıkmadan önce means before going. Use verb stem + madan önce for before doing something: çıkmadan önce, before leaving.
Sucuklu is sucuk + lu: with sucuk. The -lu ending, also -lı, -li, -lü, means having or served with that thing.
soran is sor (ask) + an: the one who asks. Add -an/-en to a verb to name the doer, like eden, the one who does.
almam gerekiyor means I need to take. Build it as verb + ma + my + gerekiyor, so the necessity is personal: my taking is needed.
görmek here means to receive, not to see. saygı görür is gets respect, the same pattern as ilgi görmek, to get attention.
yapıyorlar with no named subject means they in the general sense, like people make. It often reads as food is made here.
Market ends in a voiceless t, so the ablative from hardens to -ten, not -den: Marketten, from the market.
izlerdi is izle + r + di: used to watch. The -rdi ending marks a repeated past habit, not a single event.
korkmak pairs with ablative -den for what scares you: şeyden korkmaz means fears nothing, literally not afraid from anything.
kaynar is kayna + r, the aorist -r for a general truth: water boils, always. The aorist states facts and habits, not one moment.
sabırla is sabır (patience) + la: with patience, patiently. Adding -la/-le to a noun turns it into a how adverb.
güzelce is güzel + ce: nicely. Add -ce/-ca to an adjective to make an adverb of manner, how something is done.
rağmen (despite) needs a dative noun before it, so this becomes Buna rağmen, bu shifting to buna: despite this.
binmek takes dative -a for what you board: arabaya bindim, I got in the car, never arabayı bindim.
geçerek is geç + erek: by crossing. Add -erek/-arak to a verb to show the means, how the main action happened.
küçükken is küçük + ken: when little. Attach -ken to say while or when that state held, küçükken, back when we were small.
aldığım peynir means the cheese I bought. The -dığım ending turns a verb into a that I did label on the noun after it.
çatısından inserts a buffer n: çatı + sı + n + dan. The n slides between the its ending and the case ending so vowels do not clash.
Comparisons put the yardstick in ablative plus daha: trenden daha yavaş means slower than the train.
bırakmışlar uses -mış for something you did not witness: apparently they left it. It reports or infers rather than states firsthand.
